paragraphs.text: Intermediate junctional epidermolysis bullosa-5A (JEB5A) is an autosomal recessive mucocutaneous fragility disorder caused by mutation in the ITGB4 gene. It is a nonlethal form, unlike the usually fatal ITGB4-related epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia. Patients have mild skin blistering. Pyloric atresia may or may not be present, and urologic involvement and nail dystrophy have been reported (Mellerio et al., 1998; Inoue et al., 2000).

paragraphs.text: Jonkman et al. (2002) reported a 49-year-old woman who had had mild blistering of the hands and feet since birth. She also had nail dystrophy with onychogryposis and enamel hypoplasia. She had no alopecia and no history of pyloric atresia. Electron microscopy and antigen mapping of a skin blister showed an intraepidermal split, low in the basal keratinocytes through the attachment plaque of the hemidesmosome. On immunofluorescence microscopy, monoclonal antibody 450-11A, which recognizes the third fibronectin type III repeat in the intracellular domain of integrin beta-4, did not bind. Binding of monoclonal antibodies against amino- and carboxy-terminal epitopes was reduced. The authors considered the phenotype to be mild, with predominant features of epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

paragraphs.text: In 2 unrelated patients with mild junctional epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia, Mellerio et al. (1998) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the ITGB4 gene. The first patient carried a splice site mutation in intron 30 (3793+1G-A) and a nonsense mutation in exon 36 (W1478X). The second patient carried a missense mutation in exon 3 (C38R) and a 1-bp deletion in exon 36 (4776delG). The nonsense and deletion mutations were predicted to markedly reduce beta-4 integrin mRNA levels. The authors suggested that the missense or splice site mutation on the second allele might allow synthesis of some functional, though perturbed, beta-4 polypeptide.

paragraphs.text: In a 49-year-old woman with mild blistering and predominant features of epidermolysis bullosa simplex, Jonkman et al. (2002) identified a heterozygous 2-bp deletion in the ITGB4 gene (4733delCT). The deletion caused in-frame skipping of exon 36, predicted to remove 50 amino acids (residues 1450-1499) within the third fibronectin type III repeat of the cytoplasmic domain. Immunoblot analysis showed a beta-4 polypeptide that was 5 kD shorter than normal. No full-size protein was detected in vitro, and the 450-11A epitope was absent in vivo. The authors therefore expected the patient also to be heterozygous for a null allele. They concluded that deletion of the third fibronectin type III repeat, which is thought to interact with BP180/type XVII collagen, is pathogenic.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with mild junctional epidermolysis bullosa with pyloric atresia, Mellerio et al. (1998) identified compound heterozygosity for 2 mutations in the ITGB4 gene. One was a 1-bp deletion in exon 36 (4776delG), predicted to markedly reduce beta-4 integrin mRNA levels. The other was the C38R missense mutation. The patient had mild skin fragility.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with non-Herlitz junctional epidermolysis bullosa without pyloric atresia, Inoue et al. (2000) identified a homozygous gly931-to-asp (G931D) mutation in exon 25 of the ITGB4 gene. The mutation lies in the cytoplasmic tail of beta-4 integrin and disrupted hemidesmosome assembly. The patient had chronic skin fragility, nail dystrophy, hair loss, and recurrent urethral stenosis.

paragraphs.text: In a 49-year-old woman with mild blistering of the hands and feet, nail dystrophy, and enamel hypoplasia, with predominant features of epidermolysis bullosa simplex, Jonkman et al. (2002) identified a heterozygous 2-bp deletion in the ITGB4 gene (4733delCT). The deletion caused in-frame skipping of exon 36 and was predicted to delete 50 amino acids (residues 1450-1499) within the third fibronectin type III repeat of the cytoplasmic domain. Immunoblot analysis showed a beta-4 polypeptide shortened by 5 kD. Because no full-size protein was detected, the patient was also expected to be heterozygous for a null allele.

checks.claim: Jonkman et al. (2002) reported a 49-year-old woman with mild blistering of the hands and feet, nail dystrophy, and enamel hypoplasia, with predominant features of epidermolysis bullosa simplex.
checks.evidence_quote: The patient, a 49-y-old female, had mild blistering of hands and feet from birth on, dystrophy of the nails with onychogryposis, and enamel hypoplasia.
checks.explanation: The abstract also describes 'predominant features of epidermolysis bullosa simplex'.

checks.claim: Jonkman et al. (2002) identified a heterozygous 2-bp deletion in the ITGB4 gene (4733delCT) in the 49-year-old woman.
checks.evidence_quote: The 4733delCT mutation was heterozygously present in the DNA.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes it as a 2 bp deletion in ITGB4.

checks.claim: The ITGB4 4733delCT deletion caused in-frame skipping of exon 36.
checks.evidence_quote: resulting in in-frame skipping of exon 36
checks.explanation: Stated directly in the abstract.

checks.claim: The ITGB4 4733delCT deletion was predicted to delete 50 amino acids (residues 1450-1499) within the third fibronectin type III repeat of the cytoplasmic domain of beta-4 integrin.
checks.evidence_quote: a deduced 50 amino acid deletion (1450-1499) within the third fibronectin type III repeat in the cytoplasmic domain of the integrin beta4 polypeptide
checks.explanation: Stated directly in the abstract.

checks.claim: Immunoblot analysis in the woman with the ITGB4 4733delCT deletion showed a beta-4 polypeptide shortened by 5 kD.
checks.evidence_quote: Immunoblot analysis demonstrated a 5 kDa shorter beta4 polypeptide.
checks.explanation: Stated directly in the abstract.

checks.claim: No full-size beta-4 integrin protein was detected in the woman with the ITGB4 4733delCT deletion.
checks.evidence_quote: as no full-size protein was detected in vitro
checks.explanation: The paper specifies 'in vitro'. The claim leaves this out but is still correct.

checks.claim: Because no full-size protein was detected, the woman with the ITGB4 4733delCT deletion was expected also to be heterozygous for a null ITGB4 allele.
checks.evidence_quote: The patient is also expected to be heterozygous for a null allele, as no full-size protein was detected in vitro and the epitope 450-11 A was absent in vivo.
checks.explanation: The paper gives two reasons for expecting a null allele. The claim gives only one (no full-size protein) and leaves out that the 450-11 A epitope was absent in vivo.
